title: Miriam's tambourine (Exodus 15:19–21)
hookLine: Miriam takes a tambourine and the women dance and sing

cards: Here's a small question hiding in the text. When the Israelites left Egypt in the middle of the night, with dough on their shoulders and no time to pack, who brought the tambourines?
Someone, packing in the dark, made room for a drum. On the far shore, with the sea closed behind them, Moses leads the people in a long song of victory.
Then the text turns to someone else: a woman who may have stood in the reeds years ago, watching a basket. Now she's holding a hand drum.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."
A timbrel is a hand drum, a frame drum, the tof in Hebrew. And notice her title: the text calls her a prophetess.
She doesn't just play. She leads, and she calls the song: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."
It's almost exactly the first line of Moses's song, turned around. Moses sang, I will sing. Miriam calls, sing ye: two lines, short enough for a whole crowd to shout back.

teach.h: THE GIRL BY THE RIVER, YEARS LATER.
teach.b: Exodus doesn't name the sister by the river, but tradition says it was Miriam. If so, the girl who watched her baby brother float in the reeds now leads the dancing on the other side of the water.
There's a hard side to the song, and Jewish teachers saw it.
The Talmud tells of angels in heaven wanting to sing as the Egyptians drowned, and God stopping them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing?
Some readers hear in that story a line between thanks for rescue and joy at someone's death.
Christians sing Exodus fifteen too; some churches use it as a canticle in morning prayer. Music, it turns out, was one of the things worth carrying out of Egypt.

how: Some churches sing the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) as a canticle at morning prayer or at the Easter Vigil, and in some Christian communities drums and dancing are part of worship.

games.q: you're Miriam, standing on the far shore of the sea with a drum in your hand. Moses has just finished his song. what do you do?
o: let the men's song be enough.
lead the women out with drums and dances, and sing.
sit down and rest after the long night.
games.why: she takes up the timbrel, and all the women go out after her: "Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously."

practice: Think of one thing you've been brought through, an illness, a bad year, a long wait that ended, and give it a beat: tap your knee, the table or your chest, slow at first, then let it grow the way Miriam's drum drew the women after her.
Stand and sway if you like. If you pray, let the rhythm be your thanks to God; if you don't, let it be thanks anyway.
